## GitHub link

<https://github.com/fanimarwa-bit/Charm-Prices>

## Research question:

Do French fuel stations exploit consumers' limited attention? We study two pricing behaviours. The first is "rockets and feathers": do pump prices rise faster when the price of crude oil increases than they fall when it decreases? The second is charm pricing: do stations set prices just below a round number (for example 1.899 € rather than 1.900 €) more often than chance would predict, and do such prices stay unchanged for longer?

We then ask whether these behaviours are stronger where drivers have less incentive or ability to compare prices. We look at motorway stations, whose drivers are captive, and at stations located in communes with different income levels, measured by the median living standard and, where it is available, the poverty rate.

The unit of analysis is the fuel station. Our data cover `r format(nrow(stations), big.mark = ",")` stations observed daily from 2021 to 2023, for three fuels: Gazole, E10 and SP98. This period includes the sharp rise in oil prices in 2022 and the government fuel rebate of 2022, which makes it a good setting for studying how costs reach drivers. Our initial proposal covered 2007 to 2025. We restricted the project to three years so that the data could be cleaned and matched carefully.

The sources share no common key, so they have to be matched along several dimensions. In space, stations are described by an identifier, a postal code and GPS coordinates, whereas income is published by INSEE commune. A postal code can cover several communes, so we assign each station to its commune with a spatial join on the 2025 commune boundaries, and the station inherits the median living standard of its commune (Filosofi 2021). In time, station prices change at irregular moments, whereas Brent and the exchange rate exist only on business days. We align everything on a daily calendar and convert Brent from dollars per barrel to euros per litre.

The analysis has three steps. First, we compare how quickly pump prices react when the oil price rises and when it falls, and we look at how the 2022 rebate ( !!! AJOUTER SOURCE) was passed on to drivers. Second, we count how often prices end in each digit and test whether 9 appears more often than chance, and whether prices ending in 9 stay unchanged longer. Third, we compare stations: are these behaviours stronger on motorways, or in richer or poorer communes?

We expect pump prices to follow Brent upward faster than downward, as the "rockets and feathers" literature suggests, and we expect charm prices to be common. We also expect both behaviours to be stronger on motorways, where drivers have little choice. For income we have no strong prior, so we treat it as an open question.

## Sources

1.  **Fuel prices** (Ministry of Economy): <https://www.prix-carburants.gouv.fr/rubrique/opendata/>, yearly archives at `https://donnees.roulez-eco.fr/opendata/annee/YYYY`
2.  **Brent crude oil** (EIA via FRED): <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILBRENTEU>
3.  **USD/EUR exchange rate** (Federal Reserve H.10 via FRED): <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DEXUSEU>
4.  **INSEE Filosofi 2021**: <https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/7756729>
5.  **COG 2025, list of communes**: <https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/fichier/8377162/v_commune_2025.csv>
6.  **COG 2025, commune changes**: <https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/fichier/8377162/v_mvt_commune_2025.csv>
7.  **IGN Admin Express COG 2025, commune boundaries**: <https://geoservices.ign.fr/adminexpress>

### How to reproduce the data selection

1.  **Fuel prices:** download the archives for 2021, 2022 and 2023 from `https://donnees.roulez-eco.fr/opendata/annee/YYYY`, unzip them, rename the XML files `PrixCarburants_annuel_YYYY.xml` and put them in `data/raw`. Then run `cleaning/clean_prices.qmd`.
2.  **Brent and USD/EUR:** on the two FRED pages, set the date range from 2021-01-01 to 2023-12-31 and download the CSV files into `data/raw`.
3.  **Filosofi 2021, COG 2025 and Admin Express:** download the files from the links above into `data/raw`.

## Description of the sources 

**Brent crude oil (FRED / EIA).** The series is the daily spot price of Brent crude in US dollars per barrel, produced by the U.S. Energy Information Administration and distributed by FRED. It is published on business days only, so weekends and holidays are missing. We use 2021 to 2023 and fill the gaps with the last known value. Brent is a world price, identical for all French stations.

**USD/EUR exchange rate (FRED / Federal Reserve).** The rate comes from the Federal Reserve Board's H.10 release: the noon buying rate in New York, in US dollars per euro, again on business days only. We need it to convert Brent from dollars per barrel into euros per litre, because French pump prices are in euros.

**INSEE Filosofi 2021.** Filosofi is built by INSEE by linking income tax returns from the tax administration (DGFiP) with social benefit data. It describes the income and poverty of the population by geographic area. We use the 2021 edition at commune level and keep two indicators: the median living standard and the poverty rate. INSEE hides some values for confidentiality, mostly in small communes: the median is missing for `r format(sum(is.na(filo$median_living_standard)), big.mark = ",")` of the `r format(nrow(filo), big.mark = ",")` communes and the poverty rate for `r format(sum(is.na(filo$poverty_rate)), big.mark = ",")`. Since the income of a commune changes slowly, we treat it as a fixed characteristic of each commune and not as a daily variable.

**COG 2025 (INSEE) and Admin Express (IGN).** The Code officiel géographique is the official list of French communes and their codes, published every year by INSEE. After keeping real communes only (`TYPECOM == "COM"`), we have `r format(nrow(cog), big.mark = ",")` communes. The codes are the join key with Filosofi, and `r nrow(cog) - nrow(filo)` communes of the COG have no Filosofi data (all in Guadeloupe, French Guiana and Mayotte). The Admin Express data from IGN provide the boundaries of the communes as polygons. We use them to find the commune of each station from its GPS coordinates.

**Fuel prices (Ministry of Economy).** The French Ministry of Economy publishes the prices of fuels sold at service stations as open data, in one archive per year. Stations are legally required to declare every price change for each fuel (ministerial order of 12 December 2006), so the data are a log of price changes and not one price per day. Each record gives the station identifier, its GPS coordinates, postal code and city, whether it is on a motorway or a road, the fuel type, the date and time of the change, and the price. We use 2021 to 2023. The files are distributed as XML, which we converted to CSV. A limit is that days without a change have no record, so we carry each station's last price forward for at most 30 days to get one price per station per day.

## Key variables

**Oil and exchange rate**

-   **`date`**: the day of the observation. It is the key used to match oil prices and fuel prices with each other.
-   **`brent_eur_l`**: Brent crude oil price converted to euros per litre (Brent in \$/barrel, divided by the USD/EUR rate, divided by 158.987 litres per barrel). One value per calendar day.
-   **`DCOILBRENTEU`** and **`DEXUSEU`**: the original Brent price in dollars per barrel and the exchange rate in dollars per euro. They are kept so the conversion can be checked.

**Communes and income**

-   **`commune`**: five-character official commune code (COG), stored as text so leading zeros are kept (e.g. `01001`). It is the join key between stations and Filosofi.
-   **`median_living_standard`**: median living standard of a commune, in euros per year (INSEE Filosofi 2021). It measures how well off the typical inhabitant is. Missing for communes where INSEE hides it.
-   **`poverty_rate`**: share of people living below the poverty line (60% of the median living standard), in percent. Missing for most small communes.

**Fuel prices and stations**

-   **`id`**: identifier of the station, stored as text. It links the prices to the stations file.
-   **`fuel`**: the fuel type (Gazole, E10 or SP98 in our national series).
-   **`date`** and **`price`**: the day of the price and the pump price in euros per litre.
-   **`avg_price`** and **`n_stations`** (in `daily_national.csv`): the average price over all stations for one fuel and one day, and the number of stations counted that day. `avg_price` is our target variable.
-   **`latitude`** and **`longitude`**: GPS position of the station, in degrees (WGS 84). Missing for `r sum(is.na(stations_full$latitude))` stations.
-   **`cp`**: postal code of the station, stored as text to keep the leading zero.
-   **`motorway`**: TRUE if the station is on a motorway, FALSE if it is on a road.
-   **`last_year`**: the last year in which the station appears in the data.
-   **`commune_agrees_cp`**: TRUE if the department of the commune found from the GPS position matches the department of the postal code. FALSE for `r sum(stations_full$commune_agrees_cp %in% FALSE)` stations.

## Joining, cleaning and matching

### Cleaning

**Brent and USD/EUR.** The two FRED files were joined on the date. They only contain business days, so a row was added for every calendar day and weekends and holidays were filled with the last known value. Brent was then converted to euros per litre (Brent ÷ exchange rate ÷ 158.987 litres per barrel). The first Brent value is on 4 January 2021, so 1 to 3 January have no oil price. The table has `r nrow(oil)` daily rows.

**Filosofi and COG.** The Filosofi file is in long format, with one row per commune and indicator. We kept the commune level and two indicators (median living standard and poverty rate), converted the values to numbers and reshaped to one row per commune. Values hidden by INSEE became missing values. From the COG we kept the rows with `TYPECOM == "COM"`. Commune codes are stored as text everywhere to keep their leading zeros.

**Fuel prices.** The yearly XML archives were read line by line. We kept the station and price records, attached each price to its station identifier and saved each year as two CSV files, one for stations and one for price changes. Prices were converted to numbers and timestamps to dates. Some prices are stored in thousandths of a euro (1525 instead of 1.525), so values above 10 were divided by 1,000. We removed missing values, prices outside 0.50 to 3.50 € per litre, dates outside the year of the file and duplicates (same station, fuel and timestamp). Finally, we kept the last price of each day for each station and fuel. Over the three years, `r format(sum(prices_log$raw_rows), big.mark = ",")` price records were read and `r format(sum(prices_log$daily_rows), big.mark = ",")` daily observations were kept.

**Stations.** The three yearly station files were combined into one row per station (`r format(nrow(stations), big.mark = ",")` stations). Coordinates were converted from degrees × 100,000 to degrees, zero coordinates were set to missing, postal codes got their leading zero back and a motorway indicator was created.

### Matching

**Oil and fuel prices.** The data only records price changes: on a day without a change, a station still sells at its last price. To compute a national daily price for each fuel, each station therefore keeps its last posted price until it changes, for at most 30 days, assuming that after that the station has stopped selling or reporting. We kept three fuels (Gazole, E10 and SP98), averaged the price over all stations for each day and joined Brent by date. The result is `daily_national.csv`. Its 1 to 3 January rows have no oil price.

**Filosofi and COG.** The two files were joined on the commune code, with the COG on the left, so all `r format(nrow(cog), big.mark = ",")` communes are kept (`communes.csv`). All `r format(nrow(filo), big.mark = ",")` Filosofi communes were found in the COG. The communes without income data are the `r nrow(cog) - nrow(filo)` overseas ones (Guadeloupe, French Guiana, Mayotte), plus those where INSEE hides the median.

**Stations to communes.** The stations file has GPS coordinates and a postal code but no commune code, and a postal code can cover several communes. We therefore matched each station to a commune with a spatial join on the IGN Admin Express 2025 boundaries. Before the join we repaired the coordinates of 59 stations, where latitude and longitude were swapped and, for 11 of them, had also been divided by 100,000 twice. Five stations in mainland France had impossible values (latitudes above 54°) and were set to missing. Together with the 74 stations that had no coordinates, `r sum(is.na(stations_full$commune))` of the `r format(nrow(stations_full), big.mark = ",")` stations have no commune. Of the stations with coordinates, 13,908 fell inside a commune polygon. The other 16 are coastal stations that fall just outside the simplified boundaries, so each of them was given the nearest commune.

To check the match, we compared the department of the commune found from the GPS position with the department of the postal code. They agree for `r format(sum(stations_full$commune_agrees_cp %in% TRUE), big.mark = ",")` stations (`r round(100 * mean(stations_full$commune_agrees_cp[!is.na(stations_full$commune_agrees_cp)]), 1)`% of those with a commune). The others are flagged in the data (`commune_agrees_cp`), so they can be excluded as a robustness check. Each station then received the median living standard and poverty rate of its commune: `r format(sum(!is.na(stations_full$median_living_standard)), big.mark = ",")` stations have a median. A limit is that the boundaries are simplified, so a station close to a border may be assigned to the neighbouring commune.

**Prices and stations.** Prices are linked to stations through the station identifier, which is the same in both files.


## Graph of the target variable

```{r}
daily_national <- read_csv(here("data", "clean", "daily_national.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(daily_national, aes(date, avg_price, colour = fuel)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average pump price (€ per litre)", colour = "Fuel")
```

## Description of the graph

Average daily pump price in France, 2021 to 2023, for Gazole, E10 and SP98 (in euros per litre, averaged over all stations). The three prices move together: they rise through 2021, reach their highest level in 2022, fall at the end of 2022 and stay lower, with some swings, in 2023. SP98 is the most expensive fuel for most of the period. Gazole is the cheapest at the start but rises above E10 during the 2022 peak.
